# Coding guide

Apply these rules to every file you write or edit, tests included. Language guides refine these
rules for their language. Follow explicit user instructions and repository conventions over these
defaults.

## Write straightforward code

- Before writing code, ask whether it needs to exist. Skip work for a need nobody has shown.
- Prefer deleting code over adding it.
- Use descriptive names. No abbreviations, even idiomatic: `getUserByIdentifier` not `getUsr`, and
  no `btn`, `cb`, or `errMsg`.
- Search for an existing helper before writing one. Reuse or extend it when it serves the same
  purpose.
- Use the standard library or an installed dependency before adding one.
- Fix a bug once at its root cause, in the function all callers share, not only the caller the
  report names.
- Parse untrusted values once at the boundary and pass trusted types inward. Follow
  [ADR 0005](./adr/0005-results-and-parse-once.md) for results and parsing.
- Reject invalid states where they enter the system, and report the error there.
- Check each reason to reject in its own guard, with its own error message.

## Drop backwards compatibility by default

Follow [ADR 0008](./adr/0008-backwards-compatibility.md) for compatibility and saved formats.

- On an interface change, update its callers in the repository and delete the old path.
- Do not keep deprecated aliases, optional parameters for the old call shape, branches for old
  config keys, or re-exports of moved symbols.
- Ask before choosing when something outside the repository may use the old surface: a published
  package, API, or CLI, a user config file, or data an earlier version saved.
- If deleting the old path is outside the task, say so instead of silently keeping both.

## Keep functions small

Follow [ADR 0009](./adr/0009-advisory-review-signals.md) for size review signals.

- One function, one job. Split anything that does two.
- Review functions over 60 lines, files over 500 lines, and functions with more than 4 parameters.
- Keep related control flow and state together when splitting hurts traceability.
- Do not add inheritance or parameter objects only to meet a size threshold.
- Extract a phase or callback when its name and boundary make the caller clearer.
- Declare a helper before the function that uses it. Do not define one in the middle of unrelated
  steps.
- When a linter flags complexity, simplify first. Suppress narrowly with a comment explaining why.

## Separate logical steps

- Separate the logical steps in every function with one blank line, never two.

## Keep conditions short

- Join at most 3 checks in one condition and move the rest into named booleans or predicates, one
  per idea: `escapesRepository(file)` not `file === '..' || file.startsWith('../')`.
- Do not mix "and" with "or" in one condition. Name the inner group first.
- When a condition appears twice, replace both with one named predicate.

## Keep statements readable

- Give each statement one job. Split a line that computes a value and also decides what to do with
  it.
- Assign call chains and ternaries to named variables before using them in arguments, conditions,
  templates, or literals.
- Spread a ternary only for an optional property: `...(model === undefined ? {} : { model })`.
- Build lists with optional items step by step: `push` each in its own `if`, or spread a helper
  returning `[]` when absent.

## Comment only what the code cannot say

- Default to no comment or doc comment. Add one only when a reader would otherwise make a wrong
  change: a constraint, invariant, workaround, or surprising behavior the code cannot show.
- State the rule itself: never cite an ADR, ticket, PR, or review, and never describe the code's
  history.
- Never state a cause or measurement you have not checked in this session, even if a ticket says it.
- Never restate the name, type, or signature below the comment.
- Match the comment density and style already in the file.
- Keep required documentation and tool directives. Delete commented-out code and temporary notes.

## Write tests that can fail

Follow [ADR 0007](./adr/0007-test-placement-and-fakes.md) for test placement and fakes, and
[ADR 0006](./adr/0006-side-effect-records.md) for side-effect records.

- Make each test defend one observable behavior: an output, a state change, or an error. If you
  cannot say what breaks for the caller, do not write it.
- When code must refuse, assert the error and that nothing else changed.
- Do not assert inside a fake or callback whose errors the production code may catch. Record the
  value and assert after the call.
- Before refactoring, reuse useful coverage or add a characterization test or equivalence check of
  observable behavior that passes before and after. Do not force a failing test. For a rename, also
  check strings, docs, and serialized names.

## Decide when a module gets a property test

A property test generates inputs or call orders and checks one rule against each of them.

- Write a property test for a module when one of these triggers holds:
  - Its output depends on state from earlier calls, such as dedupe, retry, cancellation, ownership,
    or queues.
  - A bug in it was caused by event order.
  - One of its functions has a law: a round trip, idempotence, or agreement with a simpler oracle.
- When a trigger holds and you write no property test, state in one PR line why examples are enough.
- When no trigger holds, the PR needs no such line.

# Rust coding guide

Apply these rules with the [general coding guide](../../shared/coding.md) to every Rust file,
tests included. Where they differ, this guide wins. A general rule this guide does not change
applies as written.

## Names

These names are exceptions to the full-word naming rule.

- Keep a name that a standard or trait method requires, such as `fmt`.
- Use `T` for a generic type parameter and short names such as `'a` for lifetimes.

## Item order and modules

- Order items top-down: public and high-level items first, private helpers after the items that use
  them. This replaces the general rule to declare a helper before its caller.
- Follow [ADR 0003](../../shared/adr/0003-owner-folders-and-file-names.md) for module files and names.

## Errors

Follow [ADR 0005](../../shared/adr/0005-results-and-parse-once.md) for typed errors, app errors,
panics, and parsing.

- Propagate a `Result` with `?`.
- Derive typed errors with `thiserror`.
- Add context to app errors with `.context(...)` or `.with_context(...)`.
- Import the context trait as `use anyhow::Context as _;`.
- Use `expect` with a message that says why the call cannot fail, such as
  `.expect("a validated identifier parses")`.
- Never discard a `Result`. `let _ =`, `_ =`, `drop(result)`, and an unused `.ok()` all discard it.
  Propagate it, or handle the error in a `match` or `if let Err(error)`.
- In `Drop`, where no caller can take a cleanup error, print it with `eprintln!` inside
  `if let Err(error)`. Put `#[expect(clippy::print_stderr, reason = "...")]` on the `drop` method.

## Statements and expressions

- Write these forms inline: `?`, `if let`, `let ... else`, an `if` or `match` that produces a value,
  and a short iterator chain such as `names.iter().any(...)`. This replaces the general rules on
  call chains and ternary expressions.
- Name a chain with its own `let` when it is long, or when its result is a concept the reader should
  see by name, such as the rows a `for` loop walks.
- Use an `Option<T>` field for an optional value. The general spread rules do not apply to Rust.

## Function size

Follow [ADR 0009](../../shared/adr/0009-advisory-review-signals.md) for size review signals.
Do not split an exhaustive `match` only to meet them.

## Ownership

- Borrow a view to read: take `&str`, `&[T]`, and `&Path`, not `&String`, `&Vec<T>`, and `&PathBuf`.
- Take an owned value, such as `String`, `Vec<T>`, or `PathBuf`, when the function keeps it. Do not
  borrow and then clone inside.
- Clone on purpose. Before you write `.clone()`, check whether a move or a shorter borrow works.
- Suppress a lint with `#[expect(lint, reason = "...")]` on the smallest item that needs it. Use
  `#[allow(lint, reason = "...")]` only where the lint fires in some builds and not in others.

## Doc comments

- Write `///` doc comments only on items another crate uses.
- In a doc comment, state only errors, panics, and invariants the name and types cannot show.

## Tests

Follow [ADR 0007](../../shared/adr/0007-test-placement-and-fakes.md) for test placement, naming,
decision tables, and fakes. Follow [ADR 0006](../../shared/adr/0006-side-effect-records.md) for
side effects as records of functions.

- A test that touches the file system gets its folder from `tempfile`, never from a path built by
  hand. The `TempDir` guard must stay alive while the test uses its folder.
- Assert the error variant and its data with `assert!(matches!(...))` or `assert_eq!`, never only
  `is_err()`. Do not compare a human-readable message unless its exact text is a contract.
- Use `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]` only for code that panics on purpose.
- Follow [ADR 0009](../../shared/adr/0009-advisory-review-signals.md) for advisory mutation testing.

# GPUI guide

Apply these rules with the [Rust coding guide](../../languages/rust/guide.md) to every file that
uses GPUI. They add to the Rust guide and never loosen it. Each rule starts with its ID in the
[rules table](../../shared/rules.md).

## Roles

The roles come from [ADR 0004](../../shared/adr/0004-roles-languages-and-layers.md). A project maps
them to paths in the `[roles]` table of `stomme.toml`.

- `gpui-plain-core`: The `core` and `cli` role packages depend on no GPUI package and no `ui`,
  `kit`, or `app` role package, directly or through other packages. They use plain project data.
- `gpui-app-lifetime`: One module of the `app` role owns the GPUI application, its windows, action
  and key registration, background tasks, and shutdown. The entry point composes dependencies and
  starts that module. Every exit path, such as quit, the last window closing, or a system quit
  request, runs the same shutdown path once.

## Names

- `gpui-context-names`: Name a GPUI context `cx` and a GPUI window `window`. Put `window` before
  `cx` in a parameter list. These names are exceptions to the full-word naming rule.

## Elements

- `gpui-builder-chain`: Write an element builder as one fluent chain, with `.when(...)`,
  `.when_some(...)`, and `.child(...)` for conditional and nested parts. Use `.when_some(...)` for
  an optional child.
- `gpui-builder-size`: Do not split a builder chain only to meet the size review signals of
  [ADR 0009](../../shared/adr/0009-advisory-review-signals.md).
- `gpui-element-id`: Build element IDs from stable domain data, such as a record's ID. Never use a
  list index as an ID.

## Entities and rendering

- `gpui-update-closure`: Inside `entity.update(cx, |state, cx| ...)`, use the closure's `state` for
  the entity's data and the closure's `cx` for GPUI calls.
- `gpui-reentrant-update`: Never read or update an entity through its handle while that entity is
  being updated. GPUI panics when you do.
- `gpui-weak-parent`: Give a child that refers to its parent a `WeakEntity`, never an `Entity`.
  Treat a failed `upgrade()` as normal: the parent is gone.
- `gpui-pure-render`: Keep `render` declarative: read state, derive values, and build elements. Do
  not start work, subscribe, or change state in `render`.
- `gpui-notify`: Call `cx.notify()` once after a change to what the view shows. Never call it from
  `render`.

## Tasks and subscriptions

- `gpui-task-owner`: Await a `Task`, store it in its owner, or call `.detach()` on purpose. Dropping
  a `Task` cancels its work. Detaching gives up both cancellation and the result.
- `gpui-subscription-owner`: Store a `Subscription` in its owner, or call `.detach()` on purpose.
  Dropping a `Subscription` ends it.
- `gpui-no-discard-binding`: Never write `let _ =` on a `Task` or `Subscription`. `_` drops it at
  once, and `let _task = ...` keeps it only to the end of the scope.
- `gpui-stale-result`: When background work finishes, check that the state it started from is still
  current, such as the same selected item. Drop the result when it is not.

## Clippy bans

- `gpui-required-ban`: Keep each GPUI `disallowed-methods` ban that stomme requires in
  `clippy.toml`, with its reason. Add your own bans next to them.

# gpui-component guide

Apply these rules with the [GPUI guide](../gpui/guide.md) to every file that uses gpui-component.
They add to that guide and never loosen it. Each rule starts with its ID in the
[rules table](../../shared/rules.md).

The `kit` role comes from [ADR 0004](../../shared/adr/0004-roles-languages-and-layers.md). A
project maps it to a path in the `[roles]` table of `stomme.toml`.

- `gpui-component-kit`: Only the `kit` role imports gpui-component. Other code uses the project's
  own types for widgets, themes, and events, and the `kit` role translates between them and
  component types. GPUI layout and rendering types may be used throughout the `ui` role. A switch
  to a fork or another component library then changes the `kit` role only. The check is partial:
  it sees direct dependencies only, not components reached through a bundle crate such as
  `gpui-kit`.

Also apply the rules in the project's AGENTS.md and the decisions in docs/adr/ that cover the change. Read them with file_read.
